# **How to use this template** {#how-to-use-this-template}

1. Copy this file and rename it Technique\_\<yourID\>\_\<shortname\>.docx, for example Technique\_T3\_graph\_rebuild.docx.

2. Fill every shaded cell. If a metric does not apply to your technique, write N/A and say why in the notes, rather than leaving it blank.

3. Use the exact units printed next to each field. Convert before entering; do not enter a different unit.

4. Run on the shared specimen set and the frozen model and settings named in Section 1\. If you deviated, record it in Section 7; an undocumented deviation invalidates the row.

5. Return the completed template, your per-specimen results file, and your raw execution traces to the coordinating author.

# **3\. Method: Steps You Executed** {#3.-method:-steps-you-executed}

List the concrete steps your technique performs, in order, from loading the CT to emitting the flagged defect list. Every technique must ultimately produce the same three artifacts: a flagged defective-strut list scored against ground truth, a segmentation mask (if your technique produces one), and a complete execution trace. Add or remove rows as needed.

| Step | Action performed | What it does | Artifact / metric it produces |
| :---- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 1 | Load & Normalize | Load the CT Tiff stack and even out the brightness so both sides of every slice look the same. | Normalized CT Tiff stack |
| 2 | Segmentation | Use Otsu thresholding to separate struts from background, then clean up small specks. | Segmented (binary) Tiff stack; segmentation mask for IoU / Dice |
| 3 | Lattice Detection | Measure how the lattice repeats in 3D directly from the scan. No design file is used. | Lattice spacing and orientation |
| 4 | Neighbour Voting | Compare each point with the same point in the surrounding repeated cells to predict where material should be. | Expected-material volume |
| 5 | Gap Detection | Find places where the neighbours expect material but the scan has none, and group them into 3D gaps. | Candidate gaps (380 on this specimen) |
| 6 | False-Alarm Filter | Use a machine-learning classifier to remove candidate gaps caused by noise, bent struts or scan artifacts. | Confirmed gaps |
| 7 | Strut Classification | Match each confirmed gap to its strut and measure how much is gone: 85% or more is missing, less is broken. | Flagged defective-strut list: `defects.csv`, `defects_map.json` (87 missing, 74 broken) |
| 8 | Output | Report the number of missing and broken struts, a 3D view of their locations, and marked slices showing each one. | `summary.json`, `defects_3d.png/.html`, `marked_slices/` (114 slices), execution trace `trace.jsonl` |

*Table 3\. Your technique's workflow. Mark which steps produce a metric input (mask, flagged list, trace).*

### ***Defect decision rule***

State, in one or two sentences, the exact rule by which your technique decides a strut is defective, and the threshold values used. This is required so a reader can reproduce your classification.

A gap is a connected region where at least half of the valid lattice-equivalent neighbours (and at least 2) have material but the scan has none within 2 voxels. It must be ≥ 40 voxels and be accepted by the gradient-boosted false-alarm filter (p ≥ 0.5). A strut is defective when accepted gaps cover ≥ 2 of 25 samples along its free length (node surfaces excluded). It is MISSING if the covered fraction is ≥ 0.85 and BROKEN otherwise.

# **4\. Detection-Quality Results** {#4.-detection-quality-results}

Enter your scores against the shared ground truth, averaged over all specimens and repeats. The definitions are fixed and reproduced here so no one computes them differently. TP is a design strut correctly flagged defective; FP a sound strut wrongly flagged; FN a genuine defect missed.

*Precision \= TP/(TP+FP)   Recall \= TP/(TP+FN)   F1 \= 2·P·R/(P+R)*    (1–3)

*IoU \= |P∩G| / |P∪G|      Dice \= 2|P∩G| / (|P|+|G|)*    (4–5)

For techniques that build a graph, also report Edge F1, the F1 of reconstructed edges against design struts after matching nodes by position. *Leave it N/A otherwise.*

| How to read these scores. A defect detector can fail in only two ways, and each metric isolates one. *Precision* asks how many of your flagged struts were truly defective, so it falls when you raise false alarms (over-flagging). *Recall* asks how many of the real defects you caught, so it falls when you miss defects (under-flagging). These two pull against each other: flag only your most certain strut and precision is perfect but recall collapses; flag every strut and recall is perfect but precision collapses. *F1* is the harmonic mean of the two, F1 \= 2·P·R/(P+R). The harmonic mean is used instead of a plain average because it is dominated by the smaller value, so a technique cannot score well by winning one at the expense of the other. For example P \= 0.90 with R \= 0.10 averages to 0.50 but gives F1 \= 0.18, correctly marking it as poor. F1 climbs toward 1 only when precision and recall are both high, which is why it is the headline accuracy score. *IoU and Dice* measure something different: not which struts you flagged, but which voxels you labelled as material, comparing your material set P against the ground-truth set G. They judge segmentation fidelity, whereas precision, recall, and F1 judge the strut-level defect decision. *Edge F1* repeats the F1 idea over graph edges, catching connectivity errors (a hairline gap that splits a strut) that barely change voxel overlap but break the topology. |
| :---- |

| Metric | Value (mean) | ± std | Notes |
| :---- | :---: | :---: | :---: |

Tokens, tool calls and cost cover the algorithm run (detection, evaluation, slice review: 8,053k tokens, 43 tool calls, $2.52) and the report update (13,790k tokens, 45 tool calls, $3.76). Over 99 % of the tokens are cache re-reads of a long conversation carried over from earlier work in the same session, so a fresh session would use far fewer.

### ***What counts as a tool call and a token***

* A tool call is one discrete invocation of a tool (segment, visualize, skeletonize, render, etc.). A retry counts as a separate call. Report the total to task completion for one specimen.

* Token usage is input plus output tokens summed over every model call for one specimen. Include reasoning tokens if your model and trace expose them; note in Section 7 whether they are included.

* Runtime is wall-clock from task start to final report for one specimen, on the hardware named in Section 7\.

# **7\. Provenance and Deviations** {#7.-provenance-and-deviations}

This section protects the fairness of the comparison. Record anything that could make your numbers not directly comparable to another technique's, so it can be accounted for rather than discovered later.

**Hardware used:**  Cloud Linux container, 2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, no GPU; 3 repeats with identical output (runtime \= pipeline wall-clock). Tokens, tool calls and cost are measured from the session transcript, priced at Claude Opus 5.5 rates ($4/M input, $8/M 1-h cache write, $0.20/M cache read, $20/M output).  *(CPU/GPU, for runtime context)*

**Reasoning tokens included in token count?**  Yes (billed output tokens include reasoning)  *(yes / no)*

**Any deviation from the frozen model/settings?**  Unified DSC input (tif, ct\_registered JSON, 0.stl) for specimen 0.5 % dash-1; one specimen, so ± std is the spread over five 152-slice z-blocks. The detector reads only the tif. Reference (evaluation only): the print is a 0 % defect design, so every strut the CT shows ≥ 85 % absent is missing and every strut with no connected material between its nodes is broken. The y-max build-plate face is absent in the specimen; its 1,008 struts (324 missing, 642 broken, 42 sound) are excluded from the headline. With them included: P 0.944, R 0.131, F1 0.230. The GBM false-alarm filter was trained on this specimen (leave-z-block-out) with labels from an earlier reference that also used the 0.5 % STL. Model: Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5), default settings; to be confirmed against the coordinator's frozen config.  *(describe or 'none')*

**Registration method (if any):**  Detector: none (self-referential). Scoring only: the unified ct\_registered JSON, with nodes snapped to the CT node blobs (median shift 1.0 vox, max 5)

**Known limitations of your technique:**  Misses 42 defective struts (39 broken), 32 of them on the lattice's outer faces where few neighbours vote; does not flag the absent build-plate face; hides hairline breaks under \~2 voxels. 9 false alarms, all flagged broken. The noisy top/bottom slices are unreliable. The false-alarm filter is trained on a single specimen.

# **Appendix A. Run Outputs (unified DSC input)** {#appendix-a.-run-outputs}

**Result: 87 missing struts and 74 broken struts** (161 defective struts) in specimen 210127 0.5 % dash-1.

**Input.** The detector reads only the CT scan, data/210127\_Brian\_Tran\_strut\_lattices\_0point5dash1 1 Slices.tif. The evaluation reference uses the same scan and data/210127\_Brian\_Tran\_strut\_lattices\_0point5dash1 1 Slices.ct\_registered.json, with the print treated as a 0 % defect design (0.stl): every strut the CT shows ≥ 85 % absent is missing, and every strut with no connected material between its two nodes is broken.

**Run.** `python -m src.strut_defects.pipeline run --input "data/210127_Brian_Tran_strut_lattices_0point5dash1 1 Slices.tif" --out results/0point5dash1` (or the strut-defect-run skill in Claude Code). 134.9 ± 1.4 s over 3 repeats, identical output each time.

**Output files** (results/0point5dash1/): summary.json (counts); defects.csv and defects\_map.json (one entry per defect, linked to its marked slice); defects\_3d.png and defects\_3d.html (3-D view); marked\_slices/ (114 PNG slices with a 6 × 6 grid); marked\_slices\_viewer\_rgb.npy (slideshow); trace.jsonl (execution trace); review.md (visual review); score.json (evaluation).
